title_original: Sharjah Film Festival Expands Opportunities for Young Filmmakers: ‘There Is No Shortage of Talent’
editorial_title_zh: 沙迦电影节为年轻电影人拓展机遇：“从来不缺人才”

article_text:
“Learning how to make a film is one thing, but getting that film produced and seen by an audience is a completely different challenge,” Sharjah Intl. Film Festival for Children and Youth director Sheikha Jawaher bint Abdullah Al Qasimi tells Variety . “This is where many talented young filmmakers struggle, particularly when they don’t have access to producers, funding or the right industry contacts.”

As SIFF heads into its 13th edition, running Oct. 26-Oct. 31, the festival is putting greater emphasis on trying to close that gap. This year, that includes an Industry Hub and the return of its Film Pitching Session, launched in 2025, to connect emerging filmmakers with potential funders and industry partners. The initiative doubles in size this year, with six projects selected, up from three in the inaugural edition. A new Festival Ambassadors Program, meanwhile, brings former Junior Jurors back to the festival.

Related Stories

'Slow Horses' Director on Season 6 and That Final Jack Lowden Scene: 'We Had Two Endings and One of Them Was Happy'

See-Saw Films Heads on Mediawan Sale, Why ‘Tenzing’ Was Their ‘Most Challenging’ Movie Yet and the ‘World Building’ Potential of ‘Slow Horses’ and ‘The NeverEnding Story’

“We want to give them opportunities to learn, participate and eventually become part of the industry themselves,” Al Qasimi says. “I want SIFF to be somewhere a child can discover cinema for the first time and, years later, return as a filmmaker with a story of their own.”

It’s an evolution for a festival whose mandate has long centered on exposing children and young people to films, cultures and diverse perspectives from around the world. This year, SIFF received 1,802 submissions from 72 countries, selecting 71 films from 38 countries for its official program. Brunei, Burkina Faso and Mauritania will be represented for the first time, while a new out-of-competition section adds eight additional titles to the lineup.

For Al Qasimi, the need for that industry focus is clear. “I don’t think there is a shortage of talent or interesting stories in the Arab world,” she stresses. “The challenge is often what happens after they develop those ideas. They may have the skills to make a film, but they don’t necessarily know how to approach a producer, secure financing, navigate the festival circuit or find distribution opportunities.”

“Financing is certainly a challenge,” she adds, “but I believe access to the right people and professional guidance is just as important. A filmmaker might have a wonderful script, but without understanding the business side of cinema, it can be difficult to move forward.”

Closing that gap is the very purpose of the Industry Hub, which gives up-and-coming filmmakers opportunities to meet industry professionals, discuss their projects, and better understand how to bring them to the screen. The pitching session is open to filmmakers and producers aged 18 and above of any nationality. Projects must be aimed at children or young audiences, but can be at any stage of development, from concept through post-production.

The session is not a competition and will not award a cash prize. Instead, the emphasis is on cultivating relationships that could lead to financing, production support or future collaborations.

“Sometimes, one meeting with the right person can make a real difference to a young filmmaker’s career,” Al Qasimi notes.

SIFF is also looking to maintain its relationship with participants well before they reach that professional stage. Its Junior Jurors, aged 12 to 20, evaluate films in the Child and Youth-Made Film Competition. The new Festival Ambassadors Program gives former jurors a way to remain involved, connecting with younger participants and contributing ideas to future programs.

“We didn’t want the relationship with our young participants to end once their time on the jury was over,” Al Qasimi explains. “I would love to see some of them eventually return as filmmakers, mentors or industry professionals.”

That longer-term approach comes as Sharjah’s wider film and media sector is expanding, including growing production infrastructure at Sharjah Media City, or Shams .

“There is considerable potential for collaboration between festivals, production facilities, educational institutions and creative organisations in Sharjah,” Al Qasimi notes. “We all have different roles, but ultimately we’re working toward developing creative talent and strengthening the local industry.”

International exchange is also a focus of this year’s edition. Italy is the Country of Honor, with a program that includes an Oct. 30 Green Carpet screening of Fabrizio Cattani’s “Forever With You.” Al Qasimi hopes the focus will foster exchange between emerging Italian and Emirati filmmakers, from storytelling and creative approaches to production experience.

“I would like SIFF to become a festival that international filmmakers actively seek out, not only to screen their work, but also to discover new voices from the UAE and the wider Arab region.”

That international outlook goes hand in hand with ensuring young Arab audiences can recognize their own experiences on screen.

“I want a child in Sharjah to watch a film from South Korea, Italy or France and discover something new about the world,” she says. “But I also want that same child to see an Arabic film and recognize a familiar language, family experience or cultural tradition.”

Beyond its film program, this year’s edition includes workshops spanning animation, filmmaking, content creation and the use of artificial intelligence in pre-production. A new Mobile Cinema Bus, meanwhile, will bring short-film screenings to neighborhoods across Sharjah.

“For those who do want to pursue filmmaking,” Al Qasimi says, “we want SIFF to remain part of their journey, from their first experience of cinema to their first professional opportunities.”

展览现场，位于纽约市的维拉利斯特艺术与政治中心（摄影：丹妮拉·迈耶 /", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Hyperallergic )", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "10月5日，星期一，也就是那场充满争议的第一轮投票将巴西总统大选推入决胜轮的第二天，罗萨娜·保利诺坐在新学院的阿诺德和希拉·阿伦森画廊里，身旁是一面挂着她天然颜料画作的墙壁，上面画着蜷缩在种子内的小巧人物。她立刻指出，大多数都只是习作；只有2幅算作作品。她会撕掉那些不符合她标准的画作——或者说过去一直是这样，直到她的工作室助手开始为她的档案库藏起那些被废弃的画作。保利诺承认自己是个完美主义者；在她手中，精准是一种尊重。", "links": [{"text": "runoff", "url": "https://apnews.com/article/brazil-elections-lula-flavio-bolsonaro-laydown-c194f8965632c8af9bcc4e7a3716cd7c?ref=hyperallergic.com"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为第一位在巴西获得视觉艺术博士学位的非裔巴西女性，保利诺将殖民地过去视为祖国现实中的一股活跃力量，这股力量最显眼地体现在针对黑人（尤其是女性）的暴力之中，无论是以档案形式还是字面意义上的暴力。由维拉利斯特艺术与政治中心主办的她的个人展览 ¿História Natural? 正在展出，展期至11月1日止。展览以同名2016年艺术家书为核心，该书为保利诺赢得了2025–27年度简·隆巴德艺术与社会正义奖以及25,000美元的奖金。书页将麻胶版画和干刻画与为哈佛大学自然主义者路易斯·阿加西斯1865–66年巴西考察拍摄的经修改照片版画结合在一起，拼贴并缝制在纸张和织物上。没有什么是随意的；连字体都浸透着意图。“这段历史是肮脏的，”她在翻阅书页时说道。", "links": [{"text": "colonial past as an active force", "url": "https://hyperallergic.com/rosana-paulino-threads-through-painful-histories/"}, {"text": "¿História Natural?", "url": "https://www.veralistcenter.org/exhibitions/rosana-paulino-historia-natural?ref=hyperallergic.com"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "今年，由黛安娜·利马策划的巴西威尼斯双年展国家馆，采用了保利诺2024年同名画作的标题：Comigo ninguém pode（“谁也打不倒我”）。这个短语很适合她：在国家历史问题上，她毫不退让。作为多年的教师，保利诺充满耐心，她更倾向于解释而非辩护自己的立场。她逆着档案创造者的意图去解读档案。在下文的对话中，她也请你这样做。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这篇访谈由作者从葡萄牙语翻译，并为篇幅和清晰度进行了编辑。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://storage.ghost.io/c/51/f8/51f871d8-b6be-4a73-b958-0ca4fff0110a/content/images/2026/10/C2CEE158-81CC-4A73-AE8C-D0A839229831_1_201_a.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Hyperallergic", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "¿História Natural?（摄影：丹妮拉·迈耶 /", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Hyperallergic )", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Hyperallergic：对于 ¿História Natural?，你既在借鉴又在对抗殖民者的固有形式：图解自然主义者画册。欧洲探险队来到巴西进行描绘，这些图像被带回欧洲，塑造了人们对这个国家的想象。是什么吸引你采用这种形式？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "罗萨娜·保利诺：这本书实际上是对黑人以及巴西本身如何被代表的一种论述。正如你所说，当巴西被侵略时，欧洲人来到这里绘制地图。先是旅行画家，后来是摄影。那种画册形式非常普遍：这个国家被绘制成图，然后将结果送回欧洲。我借鉴这种形式，是因为它产生了关于巴西的第一批图像。它是这本画册的参考。为什么要这样做？我认为这才是真正的问题。因为巴西是一个从未真正审视过自己的国家。巴西经常使用欧洲人制作的那些图像来代表自己，而没有进行批判性审视。当我还是个大约12岁的学生时，这些图像在学校课本里随处可见。它们并不是巴西人为了理解什么是巴西而制作的图像。它们是外国人为外国人制作的图像，而巴西人在没有任何批判的情况下将其带回家。直到最近，当学校课本讨论奴隶制时，你看到的依然是这些黑人的图像。所以这本书确实是从这些图像中生长出来的。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Interview

Rosana Paulino Reads the Archive Against Those Who Made It

“This history is dirty,” says the Brazilian artist, who sees the colonial past as an active force in her country’s present.

¿História Natural? at the Vera List Center for Art and Politics in New York City (photo Daniela Mayer/

Hyperallergic )

On Monday, October 5, the day after a contentious first round sent Brazil’s presidential election to a runoff , Rosana Paulino sat in the New School’s Arnold and Sheila Aronson Galleries beside a wall hung with her natural-pigment drawings of small figures curled within seeds. Most, she was quick to point out, are studies; only two counted as works. She tears up the drawings that don’t meet her standards — or did, until her studio assistants began hiding the discards for her archive. Paulino is an admitted perfectionist; in her hands, precision is a form of respect.

The first Afro-Brazilian woman to earn a PhD in visual arts in Brazil, Paulino sees the colonial past as an active force in her country’s present, visible above all in the violence, archival and literal, against Black people, especially women. Her solo exhibition ¿História Natural? , organized by the Vera List Center for Art and Politics, is on view through November 1. It centers on its namesake, the 2016 artist’s book that won Paulino the 2025–27 Jane Lombard Prize for Art and Social Justice, along with its $25,000 award. The book’s pages pair linocut and drypoint with altered prints of photographs made for the Harvard naturalist Louis Agassiz’s 1865–66 expedition to Brazil, collaged and stitched onto paper and fabric. Nothing is incidental; even the lettering is smeared with intention. “This history is dirty,” she said while leafing through its pages.

This year, Brazil’s pavilion at the Venice Biennale, curated by Diane Lima, took its title from Paulino’s 2024 drawings of the same name: Comigo ninguém pode (“No one can beat me”). The phrase suits her: On her nation’s history, she gives little ground. A teacher for many years, Paulino patiently explains rather than defends her positions. She reads the archive against the people who made it. In our conversation below, she asks you to do the same.

This interview has been translated from Portuguese by the author and edited for length and clarity.

¿História Natural? (photo Daniela Mayer/

Hyperallergic )

Hyperallergic: For ¿História Natural? , you’re working with, and against, the colonizer’s own format: the illustrated naturalist album. European expeditions came to Brazil to picture it, and the images went back to Europe, where they shaped how the country was imagined. What drew you to the form?

Rosana Paulino: The book really is a kind of treatise on how Black people, and Brazil itself, have been represented. As you said, when Brazil was invaded, Europeans came to map the country. First the traveling painters, and later photography. That album format was very common: The country was mapped and the results sent back to Europe. I drew on that format because it produced the first images of Brazil. It’s the reference for this album. And why do it? I think that’s the real question. Because Brazil is a country that has never really looked at itself. Brazil often used those same images, made by Europeans, to represent itself, without looking at them critically. When I was a student, around age 12, those images were everywhere in schoolbooks. They weren’t images Brazilians made to understand what Brazil is. They were images made by foreigners for foreigners, which Brazil brought home without any critique. Until quite recently, when schoolbooks discussed slavery, those were the images of Black people you saw. So the book really grows out of those images.

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "The 16th Gwangju Biennale , under artistic director Ho Tzu Nyen, alongside curators Che Kyongfa, Park Gahee and Brian Kuan Wood, brings together 43 artists and groups at a single site, in a journey of understanding and embracing change."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "On the surface, the Gwangju Biennale’s title – You Must Change Your Life – is a bold suggestion. Yet underneath is more of an observation, or declaration, as change takes place whether you like it or not. It happens at varying speeds and scales: at a glacial pace, as an accumulation or even unnoticed. Equally, it could be a violent eruption, with great intensity, happening in a flash."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Inspired by the last line in Rainer Maria Rilke’s 1908 poem Archaic Torso of Apollo , artistic director Ho Tzu Nyen describes a moment when the poem reframed his perception of life, and how this has been translated into the context of Gwangju. The city was the location of the 1980 Gwangju Uprising, when nearly a quarter of a million people protested against the military government in an act of resistance seen as a pivotal moment for South Korean democracy. “Rilke’s poem begins with an intensely personal encounter between one viewer and one work of art,” Ho shared at the opening press conference. “Transplanted into the rich soil of Gwangju, a city of democracy, a city shaped by change, that inward transformation inevitably opens towards something more collective… The question is no longer simply how I might change my life. It also becomes: how do our lives change one another? How does individual transformation connect to collective transformation? How do solidarity, history and shared experience alter what a life can become?”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Echoing this collective spirit, E Roon Kang’s banners and posters, Image-Poems (2026), punctuate the biennale site and across Gwangju, with four-line texts generated using the participating artworks and Rilke’s poetry as prompts, engaging the entire city in this dialogue. More specifically, the biennale is divided into five sections, posed as five different worlds of varying scales and atmospheres. article_text:
The 16th Gwangju Biennale , under artistic director Ho Tzu Nyen, alongside curators Che Kyongfa, Park Gahee and Brian Kuan Wood, brings together 43 artists and groups at a single site, in a journey of understanding and embracing change.

On the surface, the Gwangju Biennale’s title – You Must Change Your Life – is a bold suggestion. Yet underneath is more of an observation, or declaration, as change takes place whether you like it or not. It happens at varying speeds and scales: at a glacial pace, as an accumulation or even unnoticed. Equally, it could be a violent eruption, with great intensity, happening in a flash.

Inspired by the last line in Rainer Maria Rilke’s 1908 poem Archaic Torso of Apollo , artistic director Ho Tzu Nyen describes a moment when the poem reframed his perception of life, and how this has been translated into the context of Gwangju. The city was the location of the 1980 Gwangju Uprising, when nearly a quarter of a million people protested against the military government in an act of resistance seen as a pivotal moment for South Korean democracy. “Rilke’s poem begins with an intensely personal encounter between one viewer and one work of art,” Ho shared at the opening press conference. “Transplanted into the rich soil of Gwangju, a city of democracy, a city shaped by change, that inward transformation inevitably opens towards something more collective… The question is no longer simply how I might change my life. It also becomes: how do our lives change one another? How does individual transformation connect to collective transformation? How do solidarity, history and shared experience alter what a life can become?”

Echoing this collective spirit, E Roon Kang’s banners and posters, Image-Poems (2026), punctuate the biennale site and across Gwangju, with four-line texts generated using the participating artworks and Rilke’s poetry as prompts, engaging the entire city in this dialogue. More specifically, the biennale is divided into five sections, posed as five different worlds of varying scales and atmospheres. The first gallery hall is called Molecules and Me and is flooded with an amber hue from Goldin+Senneby’s Resin Pond (2026). Two tonnes of pine resin are spilled across the centre of the space. The substance is the tree’s protective toxin, immune response and repair barrier, but the overflow of the material also alludes to autoimmunity and a body at war with itself. Something meant to protect becomes altered and suddenly excessive, in turn causing harm. Similarly, dotted around the same hall rocks from the Volcanoes of Jeju, which are listed as participating ‘artists’ in their own right, and are remnants of a slow build-up in geological pressure that swiftly turned violent. Now frozen moments, they exemplify both an act of slow accumulation and the shock of a sudden outbreak.

Bodies and Bonds , the second gallery hall, follows on as a natural progression in scale, and explores how bodies and relationships are shaped by repeated actions, family, society, political forces, illness and ageing. It underscores that changes over a long period of time often go unnoticed until documented or challenged, and as Ho shared during a tour: “Think of the faces of the people we love, the people we see every day. Their faces are constantly changing. Yet precisely because this change is continuous, we hardly notice it.” Mona Benyamin’s single-channel video, Trouble Again (2018), stars the artist’s parents in an investigation into humour as a coping mechanism for dealing with the trauma of the Nakba and Israeli occupation. The two appear as if they are in a sitcom, complete with a laugh track, monotonously reading jokes that get progressively darker. İnci Eviner’s video National Fitness (2013) examines how modern architecture, national identity and official ideologies shape perceptions of the body, while Nursing Modern Fall (2012) delves into how modern architecture imposes systems of space and knowledge while suppressing cultural differences. The moving figures in both works challenge the constructs and controls imposed on the body through repetition and movement.

Tehching Hsieh’s written statements of intent document the artist’s five One Year Performances and Thirteen Year Plan , running consecutively from 1978 until 1999. For each performance the artist shared a signed declaration outlining the clear rules of each piece, with each requiring commitment, body and mind to complete; for example, “I shall stay OUTDOORS for one year, never go inside…” or “I shall punch a Time Clock in my studio every hour on the hour for one year…”. Each sheet of paper documentation maps the passing time in a material form and serves as a repetitive dedication to creating art and pushing the limits of the body.

Expanding the scope further, the third gallery entitled Landscapes and Learning extends beyond the human as the land becomes a marker of time – tides, agricultural cycles, changing seasons – and how in turn we learn from fluctuations. CAMP’s large-scale video installation Bombay Tilts Down (2022) accumulates footage from a single CCTV camera during the Covid-19 pandemic, as the recordings are not only a tool of surveillance but also of learning. The rooftop site looks over the city to reveal a landscape cultivated by time and warped by landmarks, roads and geographical formations, as well as its inhabitants, labour, history and memories. Nina Canell’s Necromancer (2026) is a conveyer belt filled with pebbles, bones, lighters, dice, coins and more, as natural materials and human waste revolve endlessly, trapped between the rotating rollers. The futile motion allows the objects to coexist in a repetitive cycle as a commentary on the relationships between human traces, mechanical systems and living with the land.

There is also a more sinister tone, as learning and shared knowledge can enforce predictability and patterns, be hard to break free from or see beyond – unless we actively decide to change. James T Hong’s Apologies (2012) brings together videos of political and religious leaders in a collection of public apology videos. The nearly 11-hour film layers years of regret from 200 notable figures and, perhaps through this repetition, questions authenticity and asks if it is possible to learn and move forward.

On what is perhaps the largest scale, the fourth gallery – Cosmos and Change – goes beyond Earth to the universe and encompasses concepts such as life and death. In Lu Yang’s DOKU the Self (2022), DOKU the Flow (2024) and DOKU the Creator (2025), the artist’s avatar traverses past, present and future in a moral and spiritual pursuit and test of self across time and space. Saodat Ismailova’s film Melted into Sun (2024) traces how memories survive, are fragmented and reshaped over time. Melvin Moti’s On a Clear Day (2021–26) highlights the fragility of life, as the work was developed while caring for his partner with a chronic illness. The film features frogs as the main characters, with a repetition of the phrase “now I breathe”, forcing attention to one’s own breathing, body and existence. The final gallery, much like Moti’s work, brings us back to reality in Air and Articulations . As the curators note, it was conceived more as an epilogue and a wall between worlds, with Jacqueline Kiyomi Gork’s monumental installation Not Exactly BPM (Variation Rrose) (2026) becoming this wall, literally and physically. Plastic barriers inflate and deflate to form a maze, with smoke machines and multi-channel music creating a club-like atmosphere as the experience sharpens one’s awareness of body and space.

Across the biennale, movements – whether large or small – are framed by acts of gradual repetition or sudden transformation to underline the importance of recognising the inevitable. How we experience the changes that we are faced with is one thing, and not entirely under our control. However, how we understand their implications, and what decisions we take as a result of such knowledge, is a different matter entirely. The biennale’s artists provide some useful pointers in this respect, challenging us to take personal accountability in a fast-changing world where none of us can hope to remain immune.

16th Gwangju Biennale runs until 15 November

article_text:
Ogni territorio custodisce tante storie: una trama di luoghi, segni, tracce e assenze che il tempo sedimenta e, talvolta, rischia di consegnare all’oblio. Siamo a Cutrofiano, in provincia di Lecce , nella biblioteca e nel museo cittadino, centro devoto alla ceramica, uno spazio restituito ai suoi abitanti che racconta la storia del paese e il legame profondo che da secoli lo unisce all’arte figula. In questo grande palazzo, dove piani e stanze si intersecano, diverse figure autorevoli hanno lasciato la propria impronta.

Si potrebbe citare Mario Cresci , che nel 2024 ha unito l’arte della fotografia alla maestria della ceramica. Ma l’elenco di autori ed esperienze accolti da queste stanze sarebbe ben più corposo e impossibile da riportare qui nella sua interezza. Lo sguardo si ferma allora sull’ultima mostra ospitata dal museo, che restituisce ai luoghi la loro duplice natura di contenuti e contenitori, spazi fisici e insieme depositi di un patrimonio immateriale. Paesaggi, architetture e frammenti del vissuto si fanno testimoni di ciò che è stato e custodi di ciò che permane, in una continua trasmissione tra passato e presente. Il museo diventa staffetta della memoria: raccoglie un’eredità, la preserva e la consegna al tempo che viene.

L’ultima storia affidata a queste stanze è quella raccontata dallo sguardo di Donato De Donatis , fotografo cutrofianese scomparso nel 2020, che tra la metà degli anni Settanta e la fine degli anni Ottanta ha fissato in immagini una porzione del Salento. Per oltre un decennio De Donatis ha affidato alla fotografia una personale ricognizione della propria terra e del tempo che la stava trasformando. Un patrimonio che oggi diventa racconto collettivo con La memoria dei segni: Cutrofiano e la provincia di Lecce nelle fotografie di Donato De Donatis (1975–1987) , percorso espositivo curato da Giorgio Coen Cagli, visitabile fino al 2 dicembre con ingresso libero.

Tra il 1975 e il 1987 De Donatis osserva Cutrofiano e la provincia di Lecce registrandone le variazioni. Il suo obiettivo si posa sulle campagne, sui volti, sui riti collettivi, sulle abitazioni, sui mestieri e sui segni di una cultura materiale radicata nella vita quotidiana. Le fotografie fermano un mondo nel momento stesso in cui cambia, senza conferirgli artificiosamente il carattere dell’eccezionale. Ne deriva un archivio nel quale lo sguardo personale incontra progressivamente il valore pubblico del documento.

È su questa materia stratificata che interviene il lavoro curatoriale di Giorgio Coen Cagli , chiamato a selezionare le immagini e a ricostruire relazioni, corrispondenze e continuità. La memoria dei segni si articola così attorno a tre nuclei principali: il paesaggio e le sue trasformazioni, i riti collettivi e “la crita”, la materia argillosa che appartiene alla storia produttiva e all’identità di Cutrofiano. Il rito della focara affianca i Giochi della Gioventù negli scatti del 1975; poi i paesaggi rurali, le cappelle votive, le cave contaminate dalla natura.

Le opere sono presentate attraverso stampe digitali ottenute dalla scansione degli originali analogici, conservando, dove previsto, anche le cornici di carta utilizzate dall’autore. Il processo di digitalizzazione, a partire dai negativi e dalle stampe originali, è stato seguito da Federico Patrocinio, che ha curato anche la realizzazione delle stampe esposte.

Al corpus fotografico si affiancano testimonianze e racconti raccolti attraverso interviste ad amici e conoscenti di De Donatis. In questo modo, la voce individuale del fotografo si apre a una narrazione corale e confluisce nella storia condivisa di una comunità. Immagini nate per trattenere un frammento di presente ritornano, a distanza di decenni, nei luoghi che le hanno generate, e sono quegli stessi luoghi, ormai mutati, a farsi testimoni del tempo trascorso.

La mostra è un progetto di 34° Fuso, realtà attenta al territorio e alle sue storie, realizzato in collaborazione con gli eredi di Donato De Donatis e con il Comune di Cutrofiano e finanziato da Puglia Culture nell’ambito dell’Avviso pubblico per la selezione di progetti di valorizzazione e proposte di acquisizione di complessi documentari e archivi fotografici di valore storico-artistico pugliese. Sarà visitabile tutti i giorni dalle 8:30 alle 13:30 e dalle 15:00 alle 20:00, il sabato e la domenica fino alle 21:00.

article_text:
A new exhibition and the THEA space in Groningen, Netherlands, use art to think through technology and human experience, explains curator and director Roosje Klap

Last year the Nooderlicht Biennale was themed Machine Entanglements and, including exhibitions by 75 artists across the northern Dutch city of Groningen, explored “how we now live, eat, sleep, dream and even date through technology,” says Roosje Klap, director of Nooderlicht, the platform for photography and lens-based media. The shows in one venue, THEA, focused on extraction – the “ugly monster” which makes technology, as Klap puts it – and, working in the building, she was called to reception one day. “There was this guy, maybe about 55, and he was very emotional because he had seen all this for the first time,” she explains.

“He had known about it, but this was the first time he had really seen it. That was very important for me, very touching, but then he asked, ‘Is there any hope? Because I don’t see any hope, only sadness and terrible feelings’. And that’s when I started to wonder, what’s the way out? There must be a way out, how can we escape, or what’s the antidote?” That insight led to the latest exhibition at THEA, Thinking Hands , which explores how embodied knowledge endures in our ever-more technological age.

Curated by Klap with Musoke Nalwoga, Thinking Hands includes both still and moving work, and finds quirky, thought-provoking twists on the theme. There’s Paul Kooiker’s series Talking Hands , for example, a playful look at body language, and there’s Martina Bacigalupo’s found series Gulu Real Art Studio – a series of studio portraits, in which the heads had been clipped out of the image to make passport photos. Removing the face as a point of focus, Gulu Real Art Studio throws the attention on the sitters’ hands and postures, and what they express.

Andi Gáldi Vinkó’s Sorry I Gave Birth I Disappeared But Now I’m Back explores the deeply embodied experience of early motherhood, a time in which the baby is technically separate but is often ‘joined at the hip’; Martha Rosler’s Semiotics of the Kitchen, from the generation before Gáldi Vinkó, rethinks cookery skills as enforced, internalised physical socialisation. Laure Prouvost’s Taking Care (Love letter to a fellow art work) depicts the artist as art handler, talking to a viewer as if he or she is a painting or object; Requiem for an Exit by Kvam/Oldereid shows an eerie armless robot, whose disembodied projected face and AI-generated voice speak of genocide and human displacement.

“All the thinking that is somehow stored within the body, all the knowledge that isn’t necessarily in the head, that’s what makes us human.” Roosje Klap

Klap takes me on a virtual tour, walking me through the space via her laptop; we’re 300 miles apart but she’s warm and funny, cracking jokes through cyberspace. “All the thinking that is somehow stored within the body, all the knowledge that isn’t necessarily in the head, that’s what makes us human,” she smiles, turning the laptop back to herself and reflecting on how instinctively we now use technology. And photography, of course, is part of that process.

“The apparatus is part of the body, and the decision to make that photo – yes or no – is also an embodied decision,” Klap muses. “I think it is really a mind/body-correlative decision, and I feel that’s very much at the basis of what’s at stake now [as technology expands], because we are taking ourselves out of that whole system.”

And her lively engagement with technology is important because, as well as being director of Noorderlicht, Klap is now Cultural Development Lead at Niemeyer. The Niemeyer is a former tobacco factory now being developed into a public culture and tech hub and THEA has some 8000 square metres of space in it, spread over three floors; THEA is backed by the Mondriaan Fund and support from the City of Groningen, and its mission is to explore the impact of technology via art and culture. The project is a two-year startup so far but, says Klap, she’s “here to stay”, and she is co-developing THEA with Rosa Wevers, an independent curator and senior researcher in Art & Technology at Hanze University.

THEA is also developing alongside the other initiatives at the Niemeyer, which include projects such as the AI Factory; part of an EU-backed network of projects using AI to help research healthcare and agriculture, the AI Factory aims to rethink the technology with privacy, security, and digital sovereignty in mind. “The AI Factories are being put into place as alternatives to big tech, so they are interesting and important,” says Klap. “But that’s where THEA is important too.

“That work is all happening in computers; we can help make it more visible. We can also be a critical little sister to Big Brother and the tech bros. THEA and the tech companies [which are moving into Niemeyer] are an integral part of each other.”

In fact THEA is named after a rebellious female figure; Theodora Niemeyer was the daughter of tobacco company founder Theodorus Niemeyer but, rather than pursuing the bourgeois life into which she was born in 1912, went to the Hague and became a painter. She used her inheritance to create an art fund. “I wanted to honour her, and so the programme is divided into three areas,” says Klap. “It’s a combination of making, doing and talking about art, so there’s art and technology; care and technology, which includes symposia and critical thinking; and make and technology, which for example includes hackerspace.”

THEA will be a key venue for the Noorderlicht Biennale next summer, which will be themed PLAY; the theme suggests latitude to explore computer games and gaming culture, and while Klap – who will be artistic lead – is keen to embrace these forms, she’s also thinking less literally. She wants to include Debi Cornwall’s Necessary Fictions / Model Citizens , for example, which explore Hollywood film tropes and their impact on people’s perceptions, the stereotypes which inform our reactions without us being consciously aware of them.

As before the biennale will be spread over six or seven locations across Groningen, both the city and the wider province; Klap was born in Amsterdam and studied in the Gerrit Rietveld Academie, but moved to Groningen two years ago and says it’s a traditionally radical city. “Groningen is known as the red heart of the Netherlands,” says Klap, who I interviewed shortly before far right clashes in The Hague. “Something I find really great here is that I don’t have to explain to politicians that culture is important for society.”

Thinking Hands is on show at THEA, Groningen until 01 November noorderlicht.com/en/whats-on/thinking-hands

article_text:
The Prix Marcel Duchamp jury announced Thursday that it has awarded the 2026 prize to artist duo David Brognon and Stéphanie Rollin, known for their multidisciplinary practice that spans installation, sculpture, video, performance, and photography.

The Prix Marcel Duchamp is considered France’s most prestigious art prize, with winners recieving €35,000, or just over $40,000. For the award, a jury typically selects four nominees, who show together at the Centre Pompidou in October. This year, however, five nominees were chosen —Malagasy artist Joël Andrianomearisoa, Josèfa Ntjam, a participant in last year’s Bienal de São Paulo, artist and filmmaker Laura Henno, and Brognon and Rollin—and the annual exhibition was held at Musée d’Arte Moderne de Paris due to the Pompidou’s extended closure.

This year’s jury comprised Xavier Rey, director of the Centre Pompidou, along with Claude Bonnin, director of Adiaf, the organization that has facilitated the prize since its creation in 2000; Akemi Shiraha, of the Association Marcel Duchamp; Fabrice Hergott, director of the Musée d’Art Moderne; collectors Fernando Arriola and Marie-Cécile Zinsou; artists Kader Attia (who himself won the Prix Marcel Duchamp in 2016) and Berlinde de Bruyckere; Karin Hindsbo, director of the Tate Modern; and Christophe Leribault, president of the Château de Versailles.

For the exhibition at MAM, Brognon Rollin presented the exhibition 5,376 years, 1,892 months, 1,110 days, 1,201 hours , which consisted of coin-pusher machines filled with sobriety tokens like those given to members of Alcoholics Anonymous when they achieve certain sobriety milestones.

“With Brognon Rollin, the Prix Marcel Duchamp recognises a demanding body of work that gives tangible form to what usually escapes our gaze: the passage of time spent waiting, addiction and inner resilience,” said Fabrice Hergott, director of the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris, in a statement. “The work they have created for the museum, presenting these fairground objects through a subtle installation, fundamentally shifts our perspective. It is a quiet yet tenacious statement on human vulnerability and the exploration of our inner lives.

In addition to the €35,000 awarded to the winner, ADIAF, the prize’s sponsor, provides an additional €40,000 in financial support to the nominees and their galleries, as well as a feature in a dedicated annual publication.

The Prix Marcel Duchamp exhibition will remain on view at MAM through February 7, 2027. It has been curated by Odile Burluraux, chief curator at the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris, and Nicolas Liucci-Goutnikov, curator at the Centre Pompidou—Musée national d’art moderne and head of the Bibliothèque Kandinsky.

article_text:
相国寺承天閣美術館（京都市）で企画展「円山応挙と伊藤若冲」が来年6月20日まで開催されています。今年冬には江戸東京博物館で特別展 「円山応挙 リアルの先へ 空間革命」（11月28日～1月24日）が、来年には国宝「動植綵絵」の全幅が公開される皇居三の丸尚蔵館の特別展「国宝 動植綵絵 いろどりの世界」（2027年2月4日～3月14日）が開催されるなど、今もっとも注目されている江戸絵画の二人を紹介する展覧会を漫画家イラストレーターのうるぽろさんがレポートします。

室町幕府3代将軍・足利義満によって創建された相国寺。日本の禅宗の一派である臨済宗相国寺派の大本山として、京都御所の北に位置しています。

古くから寺院は信仰の場であると同時に、芸術文化の発信地でもありました。 相国寺の僧侶・ 梅荘顕常 も文化や学問に関心が深い人物で、伊藤若冲と交流を持ちました。

そんな伊藤若冲と同時代に活躍した、円山応挙。 円山応挙は京都画壇を牽引する存在として注目された絵師でした。

現在は巨匠として名の上がる2人の作品が、今回の展覧会で響き合います。

今回、同じモチーフである鶴を見比べてみました。すると応挙と若冲のタッチの違いだけでなく、動物に対する眼差しの違いも感じ取ることができました。ぜひ会場でご体感いただきたいポイントです！ （漫画家・イラストレーター うるぽろ）

editorial_excerpt_zh: 铤而走险：克莱伯·门多萨·菲略巧妙编排了一组混合了恐怖、科幻、偏执惊悚、犯罪纪实与个人纪录片的影片，它们共同滋养了他的新作《秘密特工》。

"克莱伯·门多萨·菲略的新片《秘密特工》讲述的是一个在1970年代被巴西军事独裁势力盯上的男人的故事。但它同时也是一连串生动、富有暗示性、有时甚至奇幻的离题段落，试图捕捉独裁统治下巴西社会那种亢奋而怪诞的能量，仿佛要为那个时代描绘一幅完整肖像，唯一的办法就是借助迂回、神话、自传、类型套路，以及其他种种杂糅的电影冲动，让它们接连迸发。影片以狂欢节为背景，也吸收了狂欢节那种令人眩晕的精神，痴迷于巴西流行文化的质感；它除了别的之外，还是一座档案库，收录了当时正为这个危机中的社会注入活力的各种都市传说、报纸连载和广播节目。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最重要的是，这是一部以电影本身为实质的影片。自上一部作品、散文电影《幽灵肖像》以来，门多萨越来越关注观影曾如何是他家乡累西腓大众生活的核心要素。《秘密特工》在某种意义上，是试图让这座巴西北部城市如今已有些破败的市中心重新复活为一个充满活力的地方——用门多萨的话说，那里“到处都被幻想世界所标记”——在那个地方，商业影院和电影院这一神圣空间，比任何其他事物都更能塑造社会想象，并组织起人们对极端的、混乱的、国家认可的暴力的印象。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "门多萨正在林肯中心电影协会策划一个系列，放映9部启发了《秘密特工》的影片，持续到1月13日。门多萨在成为职业电影人之前曾是一名影评人；他的电影长期以来都在说影迷的语言，而这个系列表明，他既受惠于巴西新电影运动，也同样受惠于好莱坞类型片和国际作者电影正典。约翰·卡彭特和马丁·斯科塞斯虽然不在片单中，却始终在他的宇宙中占据重要位置；与卡彭特一样，他似乎对另类政治共同体在一个堕落世界中展开某种斗争抱有共同兴趣。与斯科塞斯一样，他共享一种执迷而累积的心态，意义本身被越来越多堆叠起来的影像和段落所过度决定，而电影人更关注这些影像和段落的电影特殊性，而非其结构上的连贯性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": Morrer）。1960年代初，巴西改革派的古拉特政府支持一些让左翼学生与农村农场工人走到一起的倡议。大约在这时，年轻电影人爱德华多·库蒂尼奥开始拍摄一部社会现实主义影片，讲述东北部帕拉伊巴州一名农民联盟工会成员被谋杀的故事。他起用了非职业演员，包括受害者现实中的遗孀伊丽莎白·特谢拉，但拍摄因1964年军事政变而中止。胶片被没收，特谢拉一度入狱，随后逃往北里奥格兰德州，以假名生活。1980年代初独裁统治日渐衰落的最后日子里，年长的库蒂尼奥找到了特谢拉、她的孩子们以及其他仍在世的演员，与他们一起重看原始胶片，并了解他们如何度过过去20年。由此产生的纪录片层次丰富而动人，探索了巴西历史上一个不寻常的汇合点，以及它对农民妇女及其家庭生活的深远影响。", article_text:
Kleber Mendonça Filho’s new film, The Secret Agent , is the story of a man targeted by the forces of Brazil’s military dictatorship in the 1970s. But it’s also a series of vivid, suggestive, sometimes fantastical digressions that attempt to capture something of the wired and bizarro energy of Brazilian society under the dictatorship, as if the only way to paint a full portrait of that era is through a mixture of indirection, myth, autobiography, genre tropes, and other motley cinematic impulses that fire off in quick succession. The film, set during Carnaval and absorbing some of its heady spirit, is obsessed with the texture of popular culture in Brazil; it is, among other things, an archive of the various urban legends, newspaper serials, and radio programs that were animating a society in crisis.

Above all, it’s a film whose substance is cinema itself. Since his last movie, the essay film Pictures of Ghosts , Mendonça has become increasingly focused on how moviegoing was once a central element of popular life in his hometown of Recife. The Secret Agent is in some ways an attempt to resurrect the now-somewhat dilapidated downtown of that northern Brazilian city as a vibrant place that was, in Mendonça’s words, “marked all over by fantasy worlds”—a place in which commercial cinema, and the sacred space of the movie theater, did more than anything else to shape the social imagination and organize people’s impressions of extreme, chaotic, state-sanctioned violence.

Mendonça is curating a selection of nine films that inspired The Secret Agent in a series at Film at Lincoln Center running until January 13th. Mendonça was a critic before he was a professional filmmaker; his movies have long spoken the language of cinephilia, and the series shows that he is as indebted to Brazilian Cinema Novo as he is to Hollywood genre films and the international auteur canon. John Carpenter and Martin Scorsese, although they’re absent from the lineup, have always loomed large in his universe; with Carpenter, he seems to share an interest in alternative political communities mounting some kind of struggle in a fallen world. With Scorsese, he shares an obsessive and accumulative mentality, where meaning itself becomes overdetermined by an ever-growing pile of images and sequences whose cinematic particularities preoccupy the filmmaker more than their structural coherence.

But what’s notable about this series—a mixture of horror, science fiction, paranoid thriller, crime procedural, and personal documentary—is not necessarily the films’ general influence on Mendonça’s style or approach, but rather how specific elements from each of these films seem to be contained within The Secret Agent . The bitten-off leg in Orca ; the corpse covered with newspapers and surrounded by candles in Lúcio Flávio ; the dusty police archive in Investigation of a Citizen Above Suspicion : in a sense, Mendonça has stitched together a collection of images from these movies and reconstituted them into The Secret Agent . One imagines him a bit like Dr. Agatha Webb in one of the series’ hidden gems, Body Parts (1991)—a mad scientist attempting to recreate a composite living being out of severed limbs, each with their own consciousness and will.

The series, in many respects, transforms Film at Lincoln Center into The Secret Agent ’s Cinema São Luiz: Mendonça has programmed several movies you might have seen if you lived in Recife in 1977. Michael Anderson’s Orca , released that year and which Mendonça saw in theaters as a child, is superficially a Jaws rip-off, but it’s really an excuse for Richard Harris and Charlotte Rampling to Bogie-and-Bacall their way through a camp Moby Dick ; the titular killer whale’s chief skill, much like that of the hairy leg in The Secret Agent , is bluntly slamming into things. Héctor Babenco’s Lúcio Flávio , a lurid and brutal depiction of crime and police corruption that was a sensation upon its release, shares with The Secret Agent a sense of the dictatorship’s ramshackle cruelty—the notion that the regime can be partly understood through the noirish vision of men driving around in a car, up to no good. Mendonça even includes stills from Lúcio Flávio and Jorge Bodanzky and Orlando Senna’s Iracema in the brief photo montage that opens the film.

But the most important (and rarely screened) film in the series might be Man Marked for Death, 20 Years Later ( Cabra Marcado para Morrer ), from 1984. In the early 1960s, Brazil’s reformist Goulart administration supported initiatives bringing together left-wing students and rural farmworkers. Around this time, the young filmmaker Eduardo Coutinho began making a social realist film about the murder of a Peasant League unionist in the northeastern state of Paraíba. He cast non-professional actors, including the victim’s real-life widow Elizabeth Teixeira, but production was halted by the military coup in 1964. The footage was confiscated, and Teixeira was briefly imprisoned before fleeing to Rio Grande do Norte and living under an assumed name. In the waning days of the dictatorship in the early 1980s, an older Coutinho sought out Teixeira, her children, and the other remaining cast members to revisit the original footage with them and learn how they had weathered the past two decades. The resulting documentary is a layered and moving exploration of an unusual conjuncture in Brazilian history and its far-reaching effects on the lives of camponesas and their families.

Mendonça is deeply indebted to Coutinho; he has said he “never really [misses] an opportunity to screen Cabra Marcado .” Like The Secret Agent , Coutinho’s film depicts a family violently torn apart by the regime, and it bears some of Mendonça’s other hallmarks—an emphasis on the place of images in the daily life of a community and even a preoccupation with the transformations of the built landscape of Recife. (In a particularly Kleber-esque moment, Coutinho revisits the site of the detention center where an activist was held in the city, noting that it became a cultural center in 1976.) But Man Marked for Death also registers the transition from a 1960s student left, oriented towards collective action, to a fractured and dispersed movement 20 years later, coming out of retreat and focused on projects of individual repair and restoration. In his brilliant essay on the film, critic Roberto Schwarz writes that in the early 1960s, “it was the future of the country that was involved, and individuals were concerned only as means within this larger context.” What’s at stake in the 1980s, he continues, is “the redeeming of existences and projects . . . of an individual nature.” Schwarz ends the essay by teasing out the film’s subtle and radical implication that in a “serious world,” the intellectual class represented by the filmmaker himself may not have a place.

To the extent that this class still very much exists in Brazil, Mendonça is one of its chief representatives; his movies have come to be widely celebrated by progressive Brazilians and international tastemakers alike. Like Coutinho, Mendonça has a deep and genuine appreciation for the dignity of ordinary Brazilians, and his films have an atmosphere of dedication and tribute to everyday people negotiating severe social turbulence. The Secret Agent , for one, overflows with sympathy for the outcasts of the dictatorship era. Its central character finds himself hiding out in Recife with a couple fleeing the Angolan Civil War, a single mother living under a death threat, a queer teenager on the run from his father, and their caretaker, a 77-year-old pistol who claims to have been part of the Italian Resistance in World War II.

But Mendonça’s work registers yet another transition in Brazilian cultural production. To the extent that he is emblematic of a generation that came of age in the 1980s, his commitment to cinema seems to have preceded his engagement with political struggle, and his relationship to popular movies has always been paramount in his sense of self. The series at Film at Lincoln Center suggests that The Secret Agent is marked as much by the noble political allegiances of Coutinho as it is by the libidinal world of genre cinema—if for no other reason than that Mendonça himself is constitutionally drawn to both. The fact that Man Marked for Death stands on an equal footing with the gory B-movie Body Parts in the filmmaker’s gallery of references—and that neither film’s integrity is compromised by Mendonça’s metabolization of it—gives The Secret Agent some of its distinct power, but also some of its uneasiness, its sense of irresolution that seems to embody the country’s relationship to its own past. Mendonça may or may not share Coutinho’s aspiration for a “serious world” somewhere on the distant horizon, in which his own contributions would be extraneous, but he relishes as his raw material the strangeness and absurdity of this world and the fantasies it has used to understand itself.

At the end of Man Marked for Death , Elizabeth Teixeira gives a rousing, impromptu speech. “How can we not fight for better days?” she says. “Whoever has a good life, let them stay out of it!” She was in her late 50s at the time Man Marked for Death was filmed, and even then she already seemed to come out of a bygone era. In the iconography of documentary photography, she’s almost reminiscent of Florence Owens Thompson in Dorothea Lange’s Migrant Mother or Allie Mae Burroughs in Walker Evans’s Alabama Tenant Farmer Wife , fixed eternally in historical memory. As of this writing she is, almost unbelievably, still alive at 100 years old. She is one of the heroes of our world, a living testament to the profound courage and resilience of ordinary people struggling against overwhelming injustice. It’s one of the unexpected and vertiginous pleasures of this series, ingeniously programmed by Mendonça, that it makes you wonder what she might think of Orca .

article_text:
Hubert de la Bouillerie , who edited films including George Miller’s “The Witches of Eastwick” and “Tango & Cash,” died Aug. 8 in Los Angeles. He was 75.

Among his credits was additional editing on the 1970 documentary “Woodstock,” along with “Highlander II: The Quickening,” “Mo’ Money,” “Doin’ Time,” “Blank Check” and “Celtic Pride.”

He also served as editor on “Police Academy 5” and “Police Academy 6.”

Related Stories

Soccer Drama 'Forza,' With AC Milan Great Alessandro Costacurta, Heads to Tokyo Market With EST N8 (EXCLUSIVE)

Family Dramas Dominate Tokyo Festival’s Asian Lineup Amid 'Geopolitical Volatility'

De la Bouillerie also moved behind the camera as a director. His directing credits included the 1996 television film “The Right to Remain Silent,” whose ensemble cast included Lea Thompson, LL Cool J, Patrick Dempsey, Christopher Lloyd, Amanda Plummer and Carl Reiner, as well as the 1997 science-fiction film “The Apocalypse.”

His wife, Debbie Robins de la Bouillerie, pre-deceased him. Earlier in his life, Hubert was married to Hilary Saltzman, daughter of film producer Harry Saltzman, who, together with Albert R. Broccoli, brought the original James Bond film series to the screen.

Later in his career, Hubert continued to develop his own projects as a writer and producer, reflecting the breadth of his interests and his lifelong commitment to storytelling.

He was also an accomplished photographer and writer. He published a novel, “Of Love and Evil: The Birth,” a gothic story weaving history, love, mystery and the supernatural.

Hubert’s family describes him as a storyteller at heart. “Whether working with moving images in an editing room, directing actors, developing a screenplay, looking through the lens of his camera or putting words onto a page, he was drawn throughout his life to creativity and artistic expression,” the family wrote in a statement.

De la Bouillerie is survived by his two children, Jacqueline Bell and Alexandre de la Bouillerie, as well as his sister Annie Goeke and his siblings Caroline Gruber, Juliette Glazebrook, Diane Cottrell, Helie de la Bouillerie and Alban de la Bouillerie.

NOTICIAS

ENTREVISTA: Aidan Gallagher es un héroe de alma vieja

Antonio G. Spíndola

“La clave del éxito es el trabajo en equipo”.

A sus 16 años, Aidan Gallagher está dispuesto a salvar el mundo. Por un lado, es una voz defensora del medio ambiente –en 2018 se convirtió en el Embajador de Buena Voluntad más joven designado por la ONU –. Por otro, es la joven sensación de The Umbrella Academy , donde interpreta a Número Cinco, un hombre de 58 años, homicida y sarcástico, atrapado en el cuerpo de un adolescente. Todo un reto para la exestrella de Nickelodeon.

Cine PREMIERE tuvo la oportunidad de conversar en exclusiva con el intérprete californiano en el marco del estreno de la segunda temporada de la exitosa serie de Netflix.

¿Cómo resolviste el modo en que un hombre de cincuenta años se comporta en el cuerpo de un adolescente?

Estudié la presencia física de alguien de esa edad. Estudié a Old Man Logan. Pero, sobre todo, cuando interpreto a Cinco tomo en cuenta el cómic original, pues ahí se muestra la cualidad tonal del personaje. Más allá de las décadas en que se mantuvo con vida, el trauma sufrido realmente lo define. Pienso en esos 45 años que pasó en un mundo posapocalíptico. Todos sus conocidos han muerto. Está sólo, desesperado y luego se convierte en este asesino que viaja en el tiempo. Cinco realmente no tiene ocasión de averiguar quién es como persona. Y eso persiste a lo largo de la primera y segunda temporada, donde él sólo intenta prevenir el fin del mundo.

¿Qué aportó The Umbrella Academy a tu experiencia como actor de televisión?

La filmación de la serie se sintió como rodar cinco películas. La calidad de producción fue la de un largometraje: cada episodio es de una hora, la fotografía es increíble y tuve el privilegio de trabajar con un reparto sorprendente. Están estas personas expertas en lo que hacen, de las que se puede aprender mucho.

¿Qué has aprendido del aura heroica de Cinco, al ser tú un incansable defensor del medio ambiente?

Que la clave del éxito es el trabajo en equipo. Al inicio de la primera temporada, Cinco es muy terco y no muy inclusivo. Siente que debe hacer todo por su cuenta, pero al final comprende que necesitará la ayuda de sus hermanos si realmente quiere salvar el mundo. Y al revés, en la segunda temporada, Cinco busca apoyo, pero sistemáticamente es abandonado de una u otra forma por cada uno de ellos. Pero, sí, yo diría que necesitamos trabajar de manera colectiva si en verdad queremos generar un cambio.

El baile en el primer capítulo de The Umbrella Academy constituye el momento más icónico de la serie. ¿Qué hubiera hecho Número Cinco de haber participado?

No lo sé. Creo que la única vez que Cinco baila es cuando tiene la oportunidad de un baile lento con Dolores. Pero fuera de eso, si él hubiera formado parte de aquella secuencia, pienso que simplemente estaría tomándose un café.

La segunda temporada de The Umbrella Academy ya está disponible en Netflix .

Antonio G. Spíndola Tengo muy mala memoria. Por solidaridad con mis recuerdos, opto por perderme también. De preferencia, en una sala de cine.

article_text:
AN EXHIBITION OF SONG CERAMICS 2026 宋磁

会場：RYUSENDO GALLERY（東京都中央区京橋2-5-9、繭山龍泉堂隣接）

会期：2026年10月16日（金）～11月1日（日）

開館時間：11：00～18：00

アクセス：東京メトロ銀座線「京橋駅」から徒歩3分、都営地下鉄「宝町駅」から徒歩2分

※詳細情報は、公式サイト（ https://www.mayuyama.jp/ ）で確認を

1905年に創業した繭山龍泉堂は東洋古美術を扱う老舗の古美術店。「RYUSENDO GALLERY」を舞台に定期的に展覧会を行っており、中でも人気があるのが今回３回目を迎える宋磁展なのだという。今回は、宋磁に加え、晩唐五代の作品など約 120 点を出陳。宋磁を古典とし、新たな美を創造した清朝康熙年間の作品も展示している。

１階から３階まで、３つのフロアに分かれたギャラリー。この展覧では、展示作品の多くをガラスケースに収めず、自然光のもと、間近で作品を見ることができる。ガラス越しでは捉えにくい釉薬の微妙な表情や、器の細部、作品そのものが持つ存在感を、肉眼でじっくり鑑賞することができるわけだ。過度な装飾を施すのではなく、シンプルなフォルムと釉薬そのものの美しさを活かした造形が。約 1000 年前に作られたものでありながら、現代の物作りにも共通する、その感覚が宋磁の大きな魅力のひとつだろう。

冒頭に挙げた《木葉天目》は、中国・江西省の吉州窯で焼かれた黒釉の茶碗。実際の葉を器面に貼り付けて焼成することで、焼き付いた木葉が漆黒の地に浮かび上がる大胆な意匠を持つ。その木葉は主に桑の葉が用いられるのだが、桑の葉は禅宗で悟りの象徴とされるのだという。

宋代には、汝窯、定窯、磁州窯など、さまざまな窯が存在し、それぞれに異なる技法や器形、装飾、釉薬 の表現が発展した。同じ「宋磁」でもその表情は多彩なのだという。様々な窯で制作された陶磁を展示する今回の展覧では、バリエーション豊かな作品が楽しめる。上に挙げた《建盞》は松江藩七代当主・松平不昧公が所持していたという天目茶碗。《青白磁瓜形水注》は、様々な展覧会に出陳されている完成度の高い名品だ。南宋時代の龍泉窯青磁の特徴である、淡い「粉青色」の作品。広く 広がった口縁部は、刀の鍔のような切れ味の鋭さを感じさせる。浙江省西南部に位置する中国の青磁を代表する窯のひとつ「龍泉窯」で作られたのが、《青磁鍔縁洗》。日本では多くの龍泉窯青磁が鎌倉～室町時代に伝来しており、特に上質な作品は「砧青磁」と名付けられて現在に至るまで愛好されているそうだ。

清朝の康熙年間には、古典となっていた「宋磁」を研究し新たな美を創造した。様々な釉薬が開発され、新たな色彩の作品も生まれていったという。「天藍釉」と呼ばれる淡い青色の釉薬を使用しているのが、上の≪天藍釉瓶≫。会場には、宋代以前、中唐から晩唐にかけて制作された水注も展示されており、釉薬の進化・変遷も目にすることができる。《白釉鉄絵花文深鉢》は、宋代最大の民間窯だった「磁州窯」で焼かれた作品。今では当たり前の「絵筆でもって器を文様で彩る」技法は陶磁、画期的な手法だったのだという。民間ならではの、形式に縛られない進取の精神の表れだろうか。下の《白釉緑彩鶏冠壷》は遼の時代、契丹族によって作られたもので、遊牧生活で使っていた皮製の水筒を模したものだという。ほかにも魚を描いた宋赤絵の文盤など、目に鮮やかな印象を残す作品が並んでいる。

宋磁といえば、器ごとに違った顔を見せる「貫入」も魅力のひとつ。その「貫入」は、陶器本来の下地と釉薬の収縮度の違いによって生み出されるわけだが、今回の展覧では３階のフロアで繭山龍泉堂の保有する「米内山陶片」（戦前に杭州領事を務めた米内山康夫氏が収集した南宋官窯の破片）などが展示されており、ベースになる土の厚さや釉薬がどれだけかけられているかなど、じっくり見ることができる。少しだけそのヒミツに触れたような気分になれるのだ。初心者には敷居が高そうに見える宋磁の世界だが、それぞれのフロアには、繭山龍泉堂のスタッフが常駐していて、様々な質問に気軽に答えてくれる。肩肘張らず、カジュアルな雰囲気でその魅力を楽しむ展覧なのである。 （田中 聡） ＜あわせて読みたい＞ ◇【プレビュー】「AN EXHIBITION OF SONG CERAMICS 2026 宋磁」東京・繭山龍泉堂で10月16日から11月1日まで 無料 日本初公開を多数含む希少な宋時代の陶磁器約120点が一堂に

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Scarlet Stallone and Fears to Fathom creator Rayll have teamed to bring the horror video game franchise to the screen. Stallone’s SRYN Productions has optioned rights to the franchise for film and television development.

Created by Mukul Negi , professionally known as Rayll, the Fears to Fathom franchise is an anthology of stand-alone psychological horror stories inspired by frightening real-life experiences. Rather than relying on supernatural creatures or elaborate mythology, Fears to Fathom builds suspense around seemingly ordinary situations that take increasingly terrifying turns.

Related Stories

Fremantle Global Entertainment Exec Chris O'Dell Retires After 19 Years At 'Got Talent' Maker

Prince William Says He's A Christopher Nolan & 'The Celebrity Traitors' Super Fan

The franchise is comprised of Home Alone, Norwood Hitchhike , Carson House , Ironbark Lookout , Woodbury Getaway and Scratch Creek , each following a different protagonist. Since its launch in 2021, the brand has developed a substantial international following. Its first installment, Home Alone , has surpassed 2.3 million downloads on Steam, while subsequent paid installments have collectively sold more than 1.25 million copies.

Watch on Deadline

“I’ve been playing video games since before I could read, and the first time I played Fears to Fathom , I was hooked. I’ve played every one since,” said Stallone. “Rayll’s games are grounded and genuinely unsettling, because the horror comes from situations that could actually happen to you. I love working with Rayll; we’re a great team, and I’m so excited to expand that world while keeping what fans love.”

“I started Fears to Fathom as a very personal project, so seeing how far it has grown and how strongly people around the world have connected with these stories has been surreal,” said Rayll. “Scarlet immediately understood that what makes Fears to Fathom work isn’t just the scares — it’s the feeling that these situations could happen to anyone. I’m excited to work with her and SRYN Productions to bring that same tension and authenticity to a new medium.”

As an actor, Stallone portrays Spencer in Taylor Sheridan’s Paramount+ crime drama Tulsa King . She has also written several original screenplays and is developing a slate of character-driven film and television projects through SRYN, with a focus on distinctive intellectual property and emerging creative voices.

A self-taught developer writer and director, Rayll began creating games at around 12 years old. He first became known in 2017 with his award-winning puzzle game Loopables . He developed the first installment of Fears to Fathom while attending Delhi Technological University and founded Rayll Studios in 2023.

Stallone is repped by Independent Artist Group and Untitled. Rayll is repped by Independent Artist Group.

article_text:
Blade Runner 2099

Michelle Yeoh et Hunter Schafer survivent les bas-fonds d’un Los Angeles futuriste, où les Réplicants ont désormais l’ascendant sur les humains. Produite par Ridley Scott, cette suite de la suite de Blade Runner (vous suivez ?) profite du format sériel pour étendre l’univers et l’esthétique culte du chef d’œuvre de 1982.

Sur Prime Video dès le 25 novembre

Eldorado

En 1975, deux inventeurs font croire à Elf qu’ils ont conçu des avions capables de détecter du pétrole. Plutôt que le scandale, la série de Tarek Haoudy et Nacim Mehtar scrute les ressorts intimes de ceux qui mentent, avec un ego masculin délétère en toile de fond. Louis Farge évite la reconstitution poussiéreuse et signe une épopée contemporaine, entre comédie de bureau et aventure.

Sur Arte dès le 11 novembre

Singapura

À Singapour, Justine, journaliste fraîchement installée avec son mari, découvre que le paradis sécurisé a ses pièges. Quand une voisine est assassinée, elle enquête et gratte le vernis de la communauté expatriée française. Adaptée d’un roman d’Elsa Marpeau, la série de Lucie Borleteau et Danielle Arbid ausculte l’élite des condominiums de luxe, surtout réussie quand Nailia Harzoune et Soji Arai déploient leur jeu.

Sur Canal+ dès le 2 novembre

Les Disparus des Argonnes

Encore un true crime ? Oui, mais qui ne se passionne ni pour un tueur en série, ni pour une enquête méandreuse. Les Disparus des Argonnes s’inspire d’un fait divers des années 1980 pour suivre deux femmes, la mère d’une victime et la sœur d’un suspect, dont les vies implosent. Alix Poisson et Anne Charrier y sont excellentes.

Sur france.tv dès le 30 octobre

The Altruists

Le capitalisme peut-il être altruiste ? Vous avez deux heures et huit épisodes pour répondre, grâce à une série virevoltante sur la chute de FTX, une plateforme d’échange de crypto-monnaies. Voici un portrait au vitriol des petits malins de la Silicon Valley que certains prennent pour des dieux.

Sur Netflix dès le 19 novembre

article_text:
In a tense saleroom with a lot of silent moments and anxious pauses—at times it felt like a courtroom, with all eyes on auctioneer Tom Eddison—Sotheby’s London conducted a slow but steady £46.1 million ($61.1 million) contemporary art sale on Thursday in a full sale room, with a £9.8 million ($12.9 million) Willem de Kooning abstraction earning the top price. The sale carried an overall estimate of £41.7–58.6 million ($55.3–77.8 million); the hammer total of £36.9 million, before the house’s fees, fell shy of the low figure.

It was a trim one-hour sale, with 34 lots, 10 of them bearing guarantees. Three works—by Damien Hirst, Anselm Kiefer, and Leon Kossoff—were withdrawn before the sale. Works by Banksy, Georg Baselitz, Jadé Fadojutimi, Lucian Freud, Gerhard Richter, and Lynette Yiadom-Boakye went unsold. Last year’s equivalent sale totaled £47.6 million ($63.3 million), led by a Francis Bacon that fetched £13 million ($17.5 million).

Sotheby’s sale on Thursday came one night after a somewhat safe but healthy evening at Christie’s that totaled £218.6 million ($289.4 million) across two sales, more than double last year’s total. The sale came during London fair week, the day after stars like Tilda Swinton and Raf Simons were seen streaming into Frieze, where many dealers reported robust sales .

“I would say the market is very cautious,” Ivana Miloradovic, art historian and consultant, told ARTnews at the Sotheby’s sale. Most of the lots, she said, “either underperformed or were at the lower end.”

The sale was led by an untitled Willem de Kooning abstract painting from 1977 that was estimated at £8–12 million ($10.6–15.9 million). Measuring 5 feet wide, it sold within estimate, hammering at £8.2 million, to sell for a total of £9.8 million ($12.9 million). The painting had last come to auction at Sotheby’s New York in 2015, when it fetched $6.1 million.

Coming in second on the night was Gerhard Richter’s 8-foot-wide Abstraktes Bild (1992), which was estimated at £6–8 million ($7.9–10.6 million); it hammered below estimate at £5.4 million, to sell for £6.7 million ($8.9 million) with fees. Thursday night’s seller picked it up at Christie’s London in 2011, paying £3.6 million ($5.7 million at the time).

The Richter was followed by an untitled dark-hued Mark Rothko abstract from 1969 that was estimated for £3–4 million ($4 million to $5.3 million) and hammered at its low estimate to fetch £3.8 million (just shy of $5 million) with fees. It last came to market in 1992 at Christie’s New York, when Thursday’s seller picked it up for $264,000.

Works by Georg Baselitz, David Hockney, Albert Oehlen, and Andy Warhol filled out the top 10, with Baselitz, Hockney, and Warhol all appearing twice.

“British sales on British soil are always joyous,” said Miloradovic, pointing to rousing demand for David Hockney’s 10th—22nd June 2021, Water Lilies in the Pond with Pots of Flowers (2021) and Butterfly Fish (1978) by Michael Andrews (1928–1995). “Everybody knows the artist, the gossip and the history. It was a homey atmosphere.”

Indeed, one of the night’s runaway successes was Andrews’s Butterfly Fish , depicting the titular animal, which hammered at £550,000 on a high estimate of £120,000 for a total with fees of £704,000 ($933,117) after an extended contest, setting a new high for a work on paper by Andrews. The artist is today less well known than his School of London peers such as Francis Bacon and Lucian Freud, but he was renowned by his contemporaries: “Mike is so economical,” fellow painter Frank Auerbach once said of Andrews. “He paints only masterpieces.”

Ottilie Windsor, head of contemporary art at Sotheby’s London, echoed Auerbach’s point in a post-sale interview. “The paintings that he did make were often bought as they were being made by a group of collectors who followed his work really closely,” she told ARTnews .” [Those collectors have] never really needed to sell and so we get very, very low supply of his work to the market; when they do come up, they really do very well.”

There were mixed results for the under-50 set, with Louis Fratino’s painting Kissing Couple (2019) bringing a within-estimate £320,000 ($424,144) and Adrian Ghenie’s The Wall (2019) likewise selling within estimate for £640,000 ($848,288). (Fratino currently has a sold-out show at David Zwirner’s London showroom.) At the same time, pieces by Fadojutimi and Yiadom-Boakye went unsold.

Getting 28 lots across the line out of 34 was still a success, Windsor argued. “Any dealer at the [Frieze] fair would be thrilled to sell nearly 30 secondary market lots.” There is both interest and money in the market, she said, “but the market continues to be selective and continues to surprise us with what it’s looking for.”

editorial_title_zh: Denis Boulze and the Sweet Life of Clichés
editorial_excerpt_zh: “Images don’t belong to us. Proust’s madeleine is the same for everyone.” Set as the epigraph of Clichés (in French, the word means both a stereotype and a photograph), Denis Boulze’s line has the candor of a confession slipped backstage, between two takes. The photographer…
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“图像不属于我们。普鲁斯特的玛德琳蛋糕对每个人来说都是一样的。”作为《Clichés》（在法语中，这个词既指刻板印象，也指照片）一书的题词，丹尼斯·布尔兹（Denis article_text:
“Images don’t belong to us. Proust’s madeleine is the same for everyone.” Set as the epigraph of Clichés (in French, the word means both a stereotype and a photograph), Denis Boulze’s line has the candor of a confession slipped backstage, between two takes. The photographer knows the recipe, having served it for years in the pages of Vogue , Silhouette and Milk , for Hermès and JM Weston: a face, a hand, a shaft of light, and the reader’s memory does the rest. A proven recipe. On Roxane Moreau’s podcast Dans le bain , recorded on the evening of his first solo exhibition, Denis Boulze readily speaks of his “candy images.” Sweet, then, and a little guilty.

The taste goes back a long way. The son of a photographer, Denis Boulze started as an intern at 16 at Studio Rouchon in Paris, where he later assisted Sarah Moon, Jan Walter, Sofia and Mauro. A tough school, and a lucky draw. In the acknowledgments, he gives his father his due, the man who passed on to him “a taste for the image” and taught him “to see.” The rest reads like a travel journal, since this “beautiful profession,” he writes, “has always been a pretext for me to travel, meet new people and live experiences that have deeply enriched me.” A craftsman’s courtesy, which also salutes his agent, the formidable Florence Moll, and the printers David Dahan and Luis Escudero, thanks to whom color printing has, as the artist puts it, “today become an essential part of my work.”

So why a book? Weariness? Remorse? A big spring cleaning? On his professional profile, Denis Boulze once let out this cry from the heart: “Help, fashion! Seeing the same photographers, the same stylists, the same models over and over, I’m getting a little bored.” Clichés answers with the simplest gesture: opening the archive boxes, cutting, pasting, layering. The bags, the bottles, the logos evaporate. What remains are bodies, gestures, postures. Claire Luna, winner of the 2025 AICA-France Élisabeth Couturier Prize for art criticism, sees in it, in her opening text, “almost a visual coming out,” and extends the metaphor all the way to the closet: the curtain has risen, “but something still lies coiled.”

What you find inside: 16 faces striped with shadow, 16 hands raised as if to stop traffic, a white dove above a red and orange puddle, starfish clinging to an ear. A moodboard? Almost. Denis Boulze works in diptychs and strips, slipping a tab of red or khaki-green paper between two prints, the way one dog-ears a page in a cookbook. A woman’s profile answers an antique plaster head; two long-necked bottles bathe in a day-for-night blue, a Morandi gone to the movies; a transparent dress floats against black, a dry cleaner’s ghost. The painted lips, for their part, are doubled, like a rubber stamp pressed twice (Blumenfeld and Man Ray have been here before).

The strength of the whole lies in its softness. Everything here belongs to reminiscence, a tune hummed without knowing who wrote it, hence the title Claire Luna chose, “Comme une chanson populaire” (Like a Popular Song). Denis Boulze embraces this shared memory, which he also claims for his series “Portrait de famille” (Family Portrait), made every summer in a former chestnut-drying hut in the Cévennes: a series “very dear to me,” he wrote, “although it is unfinished and will probably remain so forever,” meant to preserve “this parenthesis of our lives which, in my opinion, resembles a gentle poetry.” Clichés shares this slow tempo, like a family album whose members happen to be strangers.

Designed by Line Célo and printed by LONGO in Bolzano, the book has the restraint of a portfolio laid on a table at a festival portfolio review. Generous white space, airy sequences, color used sparingly and all the more precious for it. Some plates read like a catalog of forms, plaster spheres and half-moons in a Bauhaus vein; others keep a touch of glamour that Denis Boulze owns without false modesty. One could see this as a limitation. One could also read it as a form of honesty: the photographer lays out his alphabet, worn letters included, and leaves readers to recognize their own words in it.

Which leaves the question of authorship. To whom does a hand resting on a cheek belong, an eye under makeup, a glass of milk on a dark table? To everyone, answers the epigraph. To whoever looks, the book corrects. Denis Boulze has known this since childhood, and closes his acknowledgments with his father, thanked for a lifelong lesson: “the importance of looking and cultivating my eye.”

Denis Boulze’s Clichés , with a text by Claire Luna, is self-published and available for €40. To buy the book, contact Denis Boulze directly via his Instagram account .

article_text:
‘B eware … of assuming the sterile attitude of the spectator, for life is not a spectacle” scream the words of Aimé Césaire – writ large and bold by Barbara Kruger, in a giant installation, The History of Tears, that fills Bourse de Commerce’s spectacular Rotunda. Kruger’s angry, menacing, viscerally charged work – words as images, and large-scale video clips of people seething with self-hate – is a thrilling setup for Remember Me, an exhibition that promises a take on 200 years of photography through 700 works by more than 70 artists drawn from the collection of the French billionaire François Pinault. That excitement quickly dissipates as the exhibition moves on.

This is the biggest photography show ever held at the Bourse de Commerce. Remember Me has two main problems: first, it tries to say too much with too few artists. For a start, nearly 450 of the 700 or so works are by Irving Penn . It leans heavily on classical, conventional approaches, styles and familiar names, and that creates a very obvious skew in the perception of what photography is, does, and how it is presented.

The organisation makes no real sense. There are two main spaces, in addition to Kruger’s installation, dedicated exclusively to one artist. Penn is one of them. The installation looks undeniably beautiful: following the curving Ando architecture, the works have been hung like waves, expanding in undulating lines across the walls, without chronology or theme, flowing freely into the space. However, when you look closely at the works themselves, this configuration becomes very problematic. There are a large number of colonial-style portraits taken in a temporary tent studio by Penn when he travelled in Cameroon and Benin. Many of the pictures depict men and women in traditional tribal dress, and were taken as a commission for Vogue. These nations were actively negotiating independence from France at that time. When you compare them with portraits by Malick Sidibé or Seydou Keïta of the same time, they look even more like anthropological, ethnographic, extractive images by a westerner who couldn’t even communicate with his subjects.

“Primitive subjects respond more to tone than to obscure words,” Penn stated of how he directed the people who appear in these photographs. To me, that says everything about his perspective on African bodies and culture. Then you notice the rest of it: the glamorous white women who appear as pristine models of passive beauty, while all the men are mediocre-looking and wear suits. Still lifes are woven through – presumably to undo the idea of hierarchy between subjects. So, a man who looks at a vase or a plate of fruit the same way he looks at people. The camera has been instrumental in colonialism, and in cultural extraction and appropriation – including in the fashion industry, of which Penn was part. But there’s no attempt to tackle that here, to counter these visions with other perspectives.

It’s not the last you’ll see of Penn, unfortunately – his works keep popping up through the upper floor, where various major names reappear in different sections that each try to heavy-handedly explain and demystify, in an annoyingly didactic way, what photography is and how it’s made. We jump between sections on composition, abstraction, portrait and seriality, to nudes – where the women have gorgeous bums and breasts turned alluringly to the camera, and the men are small and, so we’re told to think, weak and vulnerable, with very large penises. My biggest issue here was why the sumptuous, elegant nude portrait of Zanele Muholi (by the artist themself, but not technically a self-portrait) needed a lengthy wall text, justifying the work via the western painting tradition – where none of the nudes of white women seemed to warrant one. Yet a quirky series of small 1933 nude shots by Man Ray – an erotic performance featuring the younger artist Méret Oppenheim, unclothed, and Man Ray in a suit and bowler hat – are left with no explanation about the power dynamics of the camera and male surrealism’s issues with women.

This is a show that’s too afraid to let people think for themselves. We’re told Richard Avedon’s trio of 1963 portraits of William Casby, a former enslaved person who was 106 when Avedon photographed him, elevate his subject, giving him back his dignity. They’re glaringly close and unflattering photographs that resemble mug shots. Compare them with Avedon’s smaller, slightly blurred, portrait of Malcolm X. Decide for yourself what Avedon felt, whose image is claimed and whose is handed to them.

Once the exhibition lets go of the binaries, the anxiety to overexplain, or to adhere to the techniques of photography, when it allows active participation or just to be with the work, it gets better. The looser, thematic unions between images are intelligible and interesting, such as sections on “hands” and a glorious room exploring photographs of the sea. These rooms make you feel something, and reflect photographic resonances through history in a more meaningful way. By the Sea, for example, moves seamlessly from the 19th century in Gustave Le Gray’s painterly wet collodion prints, where he spliced two negatives together, one for the sea and one for the sky, to create his perfect vision of a seascape, to Hiroshi Sugimoto and Wolfgang Tillmans’ elegiac and laconic black and white ruminations. I think about why artists keep returning to look at the sea, looking for the infinite, for continuity, for obliteration and enormity. This room captures the feeling of gazing out at the sea, the ocean’s soothing violence and impervious calm.

Photography is an inherently accessible medium, and they take it seriously in France. This show feels fumbling, and an unnecessary dumbing-down. Trying to bend two centuries of one of the most prolific mediums around these particular artists is like trying to tell the history of food through three ham sandwiches. There are more than 8,000 photographs in the wider collection: perhaps it’s more varied in perspective than appears in this show – but as it is, it shirks the responsibility of retelling photography’s history with nuance and multiplicity. Remember Me forgets Kruger’s invocation at the start.

Remember Me is at Bourse de Commerce, Paris, until 18 January

editorial_excerpt_zh: 在电视业界齐聚戛纳MIPCOM交易展买卖节目之际，ACF投资银行（ACF Investment Bank）与Deadline联合邀请了顶级高管与创作者，共同探讨经典IP如何成为打造全新全球热作的引擎。这场在ACF游艇上举办、题为《隐于显处：……的圆桌会议》
